title: reco-2pw — the mark a reviewer made survives the rewrite under it
comment: The one claim acceptance step (d) could not make, made as a walkthrough: a reviewer marks an episode
reviewed, the history under that mark is rewritten in another terminal, the index catches up, and the
review state is still there and still reachable. `docs/demo/README.md` has the reproduction; the fixture
is `python3 tools/review_state_fixture.py --out /tmp/fathom-review` (six hourly commits, one episode
each, one path each, so the row on screen is the commit in `git log`) indexed with `fathom index`.
The rewrite below is the one `mvp-500-commit-review.json` step (d) performs — cherry-pick the tail onto
`HEAD~3` and prune the objects it replaces — plus a reword of the marked commit, because a reword is the
rewrite that moves an episode id (ADR-003 §5.5) and so the only one that can prove the decision followed
it. `tests/test_review_state_contract.py` replays this file against the built binary and asserts frames.
The order is the reviewer's, not a test's: mark, render the act into the ledger, rewrite, re-index,
reopen. A ledger that is only ever written after the history moved would be a ledger nothing signs.

steps.note: open `fathom tui` on the six-commit agent history: the queue is the landing view and every row in it is open work
the timeline. The rail opens with the newest episode under the cursor and its last column is `⚑` — unread — which is the state this whole ticket is about

`x`: mark it reviewed. The rail's glyph flips `⚑` → `✔`, the card line says `✔ accepted`, and the toast names the episode, the risk and who signed it. This is the state step (d) says a rebase must not lose
the queue, to check it was an act and not a paint: one less row is open than when we arrived
quit; the session goes with it (`e1.11`)

steps.shell: out=$($FATHOM review sync 2>&1); echo "sync exits $?"; echo "$out" | head -2
steps.note: the act becomes a committable ledger entry before the history moves — which is what a reviewer does: mark, render, commit, push. `fathom review sync` is the act log → ledger hop, and it is re-runnable by design

steps.shell: export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=claude GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=claude@harness.invalid GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=claude GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=claude@harness.invalid GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null; tip=$(git rev-parse HEAD); base=$(git rev-parse HEAD~3); git reset --hard -q $base; for c in $(git rev-list --reverse $base..$tip); do if [ "$(git log -1 --format=%s $c)" = "feat: tune module 5" ]; then git cherry-pick $c >/dev/null && git commit -q --amend -m "feat: retune module 5 after the review"; else git cherry-pick $c >/dev/null; fi; done; git reflog expire --expire=now --all; git gc -q --prune=now; echo "head=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) commits=$(git rev-list --all --count) tip=$(git log -1 --format=%s)"
steps.note: another terminal rewrites the last three commits and prunes the ones it replaced — the force-push case ADR-003 exists for — and rewords the marked one, which moves its id and nothing else about it
the index catches up in a separate process: three new commits, of which two kept their episode ids — identity is author + subject + paths, and for those two none of them moved
reopen: a fresh process reading the rewritten index, which is the only frame the claim is about

the mark is still here, on the row that now carries the reworded subject. The id moved and the review state followed it on ADR-003 §6.2's `shape` rung — author plus path set, the two facts a reword cannot move — and the dead row it was written against keeps its decision so the ledger reads from either end (§6.5)

steps.shell: $FATHOM review list; out=$(echo; $FATHOM review status 2>&1); code=$?; echo "$out" | head -3; echo "status exits $code"
steps.note: and the committable half agrees with the rail: the entry is `fresh` against an episode id the ledger has never seen, re-linked on the rung ADR-003 names. `fathom review status --json` prints it as `link_method: shape` with the origin in `relinked_from`
end. Nothing was lost and nothing was silently re-decided — and every figure on this page came out of the binary
